title: What is the pyramid principle, and how does it make you sound clearer?
description: How to structure what you say so the listener gets the answer first, then the reasons, then the detail. With examples for cases and everyday work.
hook: The pyramid principle is a way of ordering what you say so the listener gets your main point first, then the two to four reasons that support it, then the detail behind each reason. It makes you sound clearer because the listener never has to guess where you are going: they know the answer from your first sentence and can follow everything after it.
body:
Where it comes from

The idea was set out by Barbara Minto, who joined McKinsey in 1963 and later wrote The Pyramid Principle on logical writing and thinking. It became the standard way consultants write slides, emails and reports, and it works just as well out loud in an interview.

The shape

  • Top: the answer, in one sentence.
  • Middle: two to four reasons that support it.
  • Bottom: the facts and numbers behind each reason.

Two simple tests keep the pyramid honest. Reading down, each level should answer "why?" or "how?" about the level above. Reading up, each level should summarise the "so what?" of the level below. If a reason does not answer "why?" for your top line, it does not belong under it.

Bottom-up versus top-down

Most of us naturally speak bottom-up, in the order we discovered things: "First I looked at costs, then I noticed rent had grown, and then..." The listener has to hold every fact in their head while waiting to find out why it matters. Top-down flips it: "The profit fall is mostly rent. Two reasons..."

Bottom-up: "So I looked at the three regions, and the North was down 30%, while the South grew a bit, and the West was flat, and then within the North..."

Top-down: "The sales drop is almost entirely in the North. It fell 30% while the other regions held steady, and within the North, one large customer accounts for most of it."

Same facts, but the second version can be understood in one hearing.

Making the middle layer work

  • Reasons must be distinct. They should not overlap, which is MECE applied to an argument.
  • Reasons must add something. "The stores are underperforming" just restates a recommendation to close them. "They account for 85% of the decline" is evidence.
  • Keep it to two to four. A short list is easier to follow and to remember. Signpost them: "Three reasons. First..."

A worked example: a final recommendation

Your analysis shows a chain's operating profit fell from $12M to $8M, and three stores explain 85% of the $4M decline, about $3.4M. Their leases come up for renewal next quarter. An answer-first recommendation sounds like this:

"I recommend fixing or closing the three loss-making stores before expanding anywhere else. First, they explain about $3.4M of the $4M profit decline. Second, their leases reset next quarter, so we can act now at little cost. The main risk is losing customers who would not switch to our nearby stores, so next I'd test how many of their shoppers also use another branch."

Answer, two reasons with numbers, one risk, one next step. If the interviewer interrupts after the first sentence, your message has already landed.

Opening with situation, complication, question

When you need a little context before the answer, for example when summarising a case or presenting to someone new, a short sequence often taught alongside Minto's approach helps: situation (what everyone agrees on), complication (what changed), question (what that raises), then the answer. "We've grown sales every year (situation). This year profit fell by a third (complication). So where is the profit going? (question) Mostly into three stores (answer)." Keep the first three parts to one sentence each.

Where to use it in an interview

  • Presenting your structure: "I'd look at three areas. First..."
  • After a chart or calculation: insight first, numbers second (see so-what thinking).
  • Your final recommendation: answer, reasons, risks, next steps (see the 60-second recommendation).
  • Fit answers: one sentence on what the story shows, then the story.

Common mistakes

  • Building suspense. Walking through your working before the conclusion feels thorough but makes you harder to follow.
  • Hedged top lines. "There are several factors" is not an answer. Commit: "It's mainly X."
  • Reasons that repeat the answer. Each reason needs its own evidence.
  • Too much detail too early. Give the numbers that prove each reason, not every number you calculated.
  • Forgetting to signpost. Saying "two reasons" before you give them helps the listener keep their place.

Practise

1. Rewrite this answer top-down: "We looked at price, which hasn't changed. Volumes are flat too. But ingredient costs rose 12% and they're 40% of revenue, while other costs are stable."

Show the answer

"The profit fall is driven by ingredient costs. They rose 12% and make up 40% of revenue, which on its own takes almost five points off the margin. Price, volume and other costs are all flat." (12% × 40% = 4.8 points of revenue.)

2. Give a 20-second version of the store recommendation above.

Show the answer

"Fix or close the three loss-making stores before expanding: they explain most of the $4M profit decline, and their leases reset next quarter, so now is the time to act." It names the decision and the most decisive fact, and it is still clear if cut short.

3. An interviewer asks, "Why do you want to be a consultant?" What should your first sentence do?

Show the answer

State your answer in one line, for example: "I want to spend the next few years solving varied business problems with strong teams, and consulting is the fastest way to do that." Then give two or three reasons, each backed by a short example from your experience.

Where to practise next

Read how to give a strong recommendation and how to speak more clearly, then practise saying your answer first in everyday conversations. Next time someone asks you a question, answer in one sentence and pause. If they want more, they will ask.
